body_text: There’s a new 007, and it’s none other than Robert Pattinson . The star will slip into the tux and pick up the Walther PPK after being tapped by Amazon ’s MGM and director Denis Villeneuve for the part of James Bond. Pattinson, 40, has proven wide adaptability across his career, and it’s easy to see why he’s a great fit for the part. He showed he’s capable of putting up with chaotic productions with ravenous fandoms during Twilight, he’s played an international man of mystery in Tenet and a swashbuckling explorer in The Lost City of Z, and perhaps most central to the mission of Bond, a pervasive theme of his career is a love of parts — from Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire to Queen of the Desert to Mickey 17 — where he shows a keen interest in risking life and limb to protect the interests of the British aristocracy. This morning the Walt Disney Company will report earnings. Many will focus on the Disney+ subscriber numbers, plenty of attention will be paid to how Disney will cut headcount and integrate AI tools into film development, and the bill for all those college football games and sports rights will be scrutinized to death. But what if, underneath all the movies and the streaming and the Magic™, an even more interesting bet on the future of the company is taking place at the House of Mouse? Here’s a trivia question for you: over the past six months, what company in the S&P 500 has traded with the strongest correlation to The Walt Disney Company? Perhaps a streamer, given how much emphasis the company places on Disney+ and its centrality to the “One Disney” strategy ? You’re close — Netflix trades like Disney a lot, to be sure — but not quite the No. 1 correlated stock. Perhaps some consumer discretionary staple, given how much of Disney’s Vault is filled by the proceeds from toy, doll, and apparel sales? Close, but no; though Nike , Visa and Mastercard are all up there. Maybe a peer, you think, another diversified studio: Comcast . Good guess, but that’s only the 10th most correlated, in fact. No, the single most strongly correlated stock with Disney over the past six months has been Booking Holdings , the company behind all those travel fare aggregators. And the reason for that is that Disney is a vacation sales company that, in order to drum up business, produces a couple of movies a year to chum the waters and get people into theme parks and on to cruise ships. It’s that last point, though, that is worth drawing attention to. Disney has launched two new ships, bringing its total fleet to eight vessels, and has a further five cruise ships on order to join the armada by 2031. That’s all to push double-digit growth in the Resorts and Vacations segment, which is the real profit flywheel for Disney. Last year, Experiences was responsible for 37% of revenue but fully 60% of profit , and the cruise liners are at the center of the strategy. That’s the number that lots of investors will be paying attention to on the Disney print today. What makes the investment in cruises so interesting for Disney is that it is an especially clever play given the constraints around the theme park business. These new ships are better understood less as cruise ships and more as floating theme parks that you can send anywhere in the world and which operate with a degree of sovereignty that is simply hard to get on a terrestrial park. Disney’s latest effort to build a theme park, the Shanghai park, was the result of decades of work with the Chinese government and a five-year construction process. All of which ended with a Disney park that is 57% owned by the Chinese state. If you’re Disney, are you thrilled with these constraints? Do you enjoy pretending that you never made Kundun so that you can get 43 fen on the yuan? Heck, even the American parks have their irritations. Disney once had the ability to install a nuclear reactor in Disney World if they saw fit; a fight with Gov. Ron DeSantis reminded the company that even Florida would squeeze them like an orange if given the chance. If you’re the Mouse, you’ve got six destinations — California, Florida, France, Hong Kong, Shanghai and Japan. Let’s say you want a seventh park. Where would you even put it, so that you would (a) not cannibalize your existing business and (b) have an affluent market that is geographically far from your existing footprint and (c) serves a market large enough to demand a new park? I’m sure the boys in Burbank looked long and hard at a map and came up short. There are probably not that many more markets that could sustain a seventh year-round Disney park. But what if the theme park could serve a region for half that time, or a quarter of that time, and then go to another region? You can’t do that if your park is attached to Florida. You can do that if you compress your park and put it on a boat. Local government starts getting ornery? Screw em, cancel the sailings from their ports. Incomes rising sharply in a country? Add them to the list, start with two sailings a year and then dial it up as the median income goes up. Fuel costs spiking? Just sail the park to them , after all every dollar spent on the airline ticket is a dollar the guest can’t spend at Disney. The cruise lines allow them to essentially do surge pricing, but for an amusement park, following the demand while maintaining the kind of autonomy that can truly only be found in international waters. title: 🧥 Nvidia loses its leather jacket
body_text: Happy Monday to everyone except those whose employers use Microsoft Outlook for email. Those poor souls, who already spend half their workday searching for emails that are definitely in their inboxes, got an unexpected break on Thursday and Friday thanks to a widespread Microsoft outage . They probably needed it. After all, Teams tells their bosses they're slacking off if they leave their mouse untouched for more than five minutes. Headlines last week were dominated by one thing. For those living under a rock, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned following a series of bombshell reports that painted a picture of a leather jacket-clad man who founded a chip company for video games, became one of the most powerful people in the world, and apparently succumbed to the temptations that came with it. First came reports that Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman who US intelligence officials reportedly considered a spy for the Chinese government. The woman’s company, Megaspeed, was reportedly able to obtain Nvidia chips in China despite export controls designed to prevent China from beating the US on artificial intelligence. (Oh, and during this time, he was also reportedly having affairs with at least two Nvidia employees.) Meanwhile, in Washington, they’re all trying to find the guy who was supposed to prevent this from happening but didn’t. Lawmakers called on Haung and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify. This brings into question how long Lutnick, who is supposed to be in charge of enforcing those export controls, will stay with the administration. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he supported blacklisting Megaspeed but Lutnick didn’t act . Secretary of State Marco Rubio (a Republican presidential hopeful), also reportedly sounded the alarms about the relationship to no avail . Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, will be interim CEO. But the transition could be awkward, given that Huang didn't always seem to hold her in particularly high regard. As recently as this summer, Huang belittled her at a meeting and called her a “deer in the headlights,” according to The Wall Street Journal . When asked earlier this fall by Wired who the most powerful women in tech were, Huang did not name her. We still don’t know who will replace Huang on a permanent basis. President Trump suggested former Apple CEO, Tim Cook. Prediction markets are favoring Ian Buck, Nvidia’s vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing. The stock has taken a massive hit from the scandal. Nvidia is still scheduled to report earnings results on Tuesday, in which it may report better-than-expected numbers, as it often does, which could potentially offer some relief. Kress will take questions from analysts, some of whom downgraded the stock this week . The market is still figuring out how to price in this juicy gossip. On one hand, the scandal shows people want Nvidia's chips so badly that they're willing to (allegedly) commit espionage to get them. And demand for those chips isn't going to disappear just because Huang is gone. On the other hand, the allegations have invited a major legal and regulatory headache for Nvidia at a time investors have been jittery about the AI trade and the public opinion on AI infrastructure has soured. Then there's the Jensen factor. Maybe Huang, the only CEO the company has ever had, has the secret sauce that a successor won't be able to replicate. As my colleague Luke Kawa points out in the EntryPoint newsletter, Huang's interpersonal skills helped bolster demand (perhaps to a fault). The question now is whether Nvidia's next CEO can keep the orders flowing without the industry's most recognizable salesman. As the Nvidia scandal unfolded Thursday, the chip company completely dominated trading activity on Robinhood. 6,184 single stocks were traded on Robinhood Markets on Thursday, and net purchases of Nvidia were more than double the rest of those 6,183 stocks, combined! body_text: It took several hours longer than expected, but the SS United States is now sitting at the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico just off the Florida coast near Pensacola. Rather than serving meals of caviar and roast duck as it did during its heyday zipping across the Atlantic, it will now form an artificial reef that attracts marlin and swordfish, and eventually with them, divers and fishermen, the Associated Press reports . The SS US was larger than the Titanic and set a transatlantic speed record on its first voyage in 1952 with an average speed of 41 miles per hour. Federal rules prevent the use of explosives in intentional scuttlings, so instead Coleen Marine, the company tasked with the sinking, removed the tanks that held seawater used to cool the ship’s boilers. Once water flowed in through the intakes, it flooded the vessel. Over 400 portholes were also removed and large holes cut into the deck. The SS US joins more than 500 other artificial reefs in the area off the Gulf coast where it now lays. Stocks fell on Thursday as Nvidia fell before recovering much of its losses and the AI trade showed resilience despite the ouster of one of the most important CEOs in the industry. In a turn of events that would have been shocking even a week ago, Jensen Huang is out as the CEO of Nvidia after his position leading the most important chipmaker in the world became untenable following the development of a series of scandals about his conduct. The move comes at a major inflection point in the AI trade, after several months of the biggest names from Intel to the AI labs to the neoclouds being rattled by earnings, the debt market, and somewhat ambiguous vibes around the ultimate value of this technology and the ultimate ability of the companies involved in the AI trade to capture it. Huang had long been the sector’s biggest cheerleader, its financier, and the guy responsible for selling the single most valuable piece of hardware technology in the whole boom. The coming weeks will reveal precisely how necessary Huang is to the action here. Consider it a fundamental test of the “great man theory of history” as it applies to business. Was Nvidia successful because of Huang’s particular vision and networking ability? Or will Nvidia be able to continue its run absent its leather-jacketed leader, because at this point it’s not exactly rocket science selling a GPU to a data center. The manner of Huang’s departure will at the very least likely be bruising for Nvidia in the short- to medium-term; the scandal began when it was reported that Huang was engaged in a romantic entanglement with a woman who had been identified as a likely Chinese intelligence asset. The incident that precipitated his actual departure — reporting that indicated this sort of behavior was not exactly exceptional, and that Huang had allegedly been involved with co-workers too — doesn’t exactly paint a great picture. Either way, now Congress is getting involved , as House investigators tend to hate it when the businessman behind the single most important piece of technology of the decade gets honeypotted by America’s primary geopolitical and industrial rival. Nvidia shares took it on the chin this week, but retail traders appear to be bullish on the company’s ability to perform well absent Huang. According to my colleague Luke Kawa and the EntryPoint newsletter , traders have been enthusiastically buying the dip here in anticipation that, however things shake out with Huang, people are going to need those graphics cards and they’re probably fine buying them from Colette Kress for the time being. Indeed, one plausible fallout of this stands to benefit the large firms helming the AI industry in the United States. The frontier labs have long argued that tough regulation of AI, especially the open-source AI that dominates China’s role in the emerging tech, is a necessity. Huang opposed that, through his desire to export his chips to whoever would buy them and his support of the open source world of models and his purchase of HuggingFace.
